sections.heading: IV-A Persistent On-Chip State
sections.text: The foundational enabler is holding the full recurrent state—32 matrices of 128 × 128 128\times 128 FP32 values totaling 2 MB—permanently in BRAM across all token steps. Unlike GPU implementations that must round-trip state through HBM every token, our state persists on-chip via static HLS arrays mapped to dual-port BRAM. The host invokes the kernel once per token, passing only the ∼ \sim 48.5 KB of q/k/v tokens and gate values via AXI. This satisfies constraint ( 8 ) and eliminates state I/O entirely.

sections.heading: IV-B Fused Five-Phase Compute Pipeline

The tiled accumulation in Phase 1 has a loop-carried dependency on the partial-sum registers. With 128 / P K = 8 128/P_{K}=8 tiles per row, the recurrence distance is 8 cycles, exceeding the FP32 fadd latency ( ∼ \sim 5 cycles), guaranteeing the HLS scheduler can achieve II = = 1.

sections.heading: IV-C GVA-Aware Paired-Head Parallelism
sections.text: The 2:1 GVA structure means each q/k pair serves R = 2 R{=}2 value-heads. We exploit this by processing both v-heads of a GVA pair simultaneously: the q and k vectors are broadcast to both heads, while each head maintains its own state matrix, gate values, and accumulators. This doubles the effective compute per q/k load without duplicating q/k storage. More broadly, all H iter H_{\mathrm{iter}} v-heads are processed in parallel: the innermost loops over column tiles and head indices are fully unrolled, while the outer tile loop is pipelined at II = = 1. BRAM partitioning ensures conflict-free access: complete partitioning along the head dimension gives each head its own bank group, while cyclic partitioning with factor P K P_{K} along the column dimension provides P K P_{K} independent column banks per head.

sections.heading: IV-D Dataflow Pipelining
sections.text: The 32 v-heads are divided into groups of H iter H_{\mathrm{iter}} heads processed per iteration, yielding N iter = h v / H iter N_{\mathrm{iter}}=h_{v}/H_{\mathrm{iter}} iterations. Each iteration comprises three stages: 1. Prepare : copy relevant q/k/v slices and compute gates g t g_{t} , β t \beta_{t} (Eqs. ( 5 )–( 6 )). 2. Compute : execute the fused five-phase pipeline over H iter H_{\mathrm{iter}} heads in parallel. 3. Store : write H iter × d H_{\mathrm{iter}}\times d output elements to external memory via AXI. HLS dataflow pipelining overlaps these stages: prepare for iteration n + 1 n{+}1 runs concurrently with compute for iteration n n and store for iteration n − 1 n{-}1 . The pipeline interval is determined by the slowest stage—compute at ∼ \sim 2,105 cycles—so the effective iteration cost is 2,106 cycles regardless of H iter H_{\mathrm{iter}} . The state array is structured as a 4D tensor indexed by [ iter ] ​ [ h ] ​ [ i ] ​ [ j ] [\textit{iter}][h][i][j] so that each iteration accesses a disjoint first-dimension slice, providing the HLS compiler with static proof of no inter-iteration conflicts.

sections.heading: V-A Target Platform
sections.text: We target the AMD Alveo U55C accelerator card featuring 4,032 BRAM36 blocks ( ∼ \sim 17.6 MB), 9,024 DSP48E2 slices, 2.73M flip-flops, and 1.30M LUTs. The design is synthesized using Vitis HLS 2025.1 with a target clock period of 3.33 ns (300 MHz).

sections.heading: VI-C Energy Efficiency
sections.text: Post-implementation power analysis in Vivado reports a total on-chip power of only 9.96 W for the placed H iter = 2 H_{\mathrm{iter}}{=}2 design—comprising 6.54 W dynamic (BRAM 1.67 W, DSP 0.85 W, logic 1.03 W, clocks 1.18 W, routing 1.82 W) and 3.42 W static. At 1.61 mJ per token, the implemented H iter = 2 H_{\mathrm{iter}}{=}2 configuration is 62 × \times more energy-efficient than the GPU baseline. This dramatic gap arises from two compounding factors: (1) the FPGA eliminates the HBM state round-trip, completing the workload faster; and (2) actual on-chip power at 12% resource utilization is far below the 150 W board TDP [ 17 ] . DSP, FF, and LUT scale approximately linearly with H iter H_{\mathrm{iter}} as each additional head requires its own set of multiply-accumulate units and state-access ports. sections.heading: VI-E Ablation Analysis
sections.text: For H iter ∈ { 2 , 4 , 8 } H_{\mathrm{iter}}\in\{2,4,8\} , the compute stage dominates each dataflow iteration at a near-constant ∼ \sim 2,105 cycles. Total latency follows the model L ≈ N iter × 2,106 + L load L\approx N_{\mathrm{iter}}\times 2{,}106+L_{\mathrm{load}} , where L load ≈ 8,800 L_{\mathrm{load}}\approx 8{,}800 – 10,600 10{,}600 cycles. At H iter = 16 H_{\mathrm{iter}}{=}16 , this model breaks down. The per-iteration interval inflates from ∼ \sim 2,106 to ∼ \sim 6,300 cycles because the wider datapath (16 heads unrolled) increases pipeline depth and routing pressure, raising the effective initiation interval of the tiled loops. The result is that H iter = 16 H_{\mathrm{iter}}{=}16 at 23,206 total cycles is slower than H iter = 8 H_{\mathrm{iter}}{=}8 at 18,978 despite having half the iterations. This identifies H iter = 8 H_{\mathrm{iter}}{=}8 as the optimal configuration: it minimizes latency at 4.5 × \times speedup while staying under 25% utilization for all resource types. Physical scaling wall. Post-implementation results reinforce the synthesis trends (Figure 6 ). H iter = 2 H_{\mathrm{iter}}{=}2 places and routes within a single SLR at 263 MHz. H iter = 4 H_{\mathrm{iter}}{=}4 passes post-synthesis timing with an identical 2.370 ns critical path but fails routing: at 77% SLR-level BRAM and 39% LUT, the design saturates SLR0 and spills across SLR boundaries, causing 88,725 unroutable signals. This confirms that H iter ∈ { 8 , 16 } H_{\mathrm{iter}}\in\{8,16\} would require explicit multi-SLR floorplanning or a larger device, and that H iter = 2 H_{\mathrm{iter}}{=}2 represents the most implementable design point at the cost of higher latency.
